extracted.intended_audience: electric utilities, environmental consultants, regulatory commenters, and EPA policymakers involved in CCR/RCRA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria EPA used to assess risks from coal combustion residuals (CCR) management practices (landfills, surface impoundments, legacy units) for the 2014/2024 risk records and to justify regulatory action under RCRA. Covers exposure-pathway definitions, modeling approaches, risk thresholds, data types, and site/practice factors that affect risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk range for determining regulation under RCRA
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA typically uses an acceptable risk level ranging between 1 × 10^-4 and 1 × 10^-6 to determine whether regulation is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA uses as an initial cancer risk “level of concern” a calculated risk level of 1 × 10^-5 (one in one hundred thousand) or an HQ above 1.0 for noncarcinogenic risks. Wastestreams or activities with a calculated high-end individual cancer-risk level of 1 × 10^-5 or higher are generally considered candidates for regulation; risks of 1 × 10^-4 or higher generally will be regulated; risks of 1 × 10^-6 or lower (and HQ < 1) generally will be considered not to pose a reasonable probability of adverse effects and generally will not be regulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure routes to evaluate in CCR risk assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific exposure routes EPA modeled in the 2014 Risk Assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate: (1) human inhalation of particulate matter from open units, (2) human ingestion of crops and livestock raised on nearby fields, (3) human ingestion of groundwater used as drinking water, (4) human ingestion of fish caught from freshwater streams, and (5) ecological contact with and ingestion of surface water and sediment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of highly exposed and moderately exposed individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: How EPA reports and interprets modeled risk percentiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risks to highly exposed individuals represent a reasonable maximum estimate and were calculated as the 90th percentiles of all probabilistic model results. Risks to moderately exposed individuals represent a more typical estimate and were calculated as the 50th percentiles of all probabilistic model results.

rubrics_metrics.name: National-scale probabilistic analysis with prevalence weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach for producing a national snapshot of CCR-related risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a combination of models to predict fate/transport and receptor exposures, use site-specific data where available, supplement with regional/national data to fill gaps, and weight risks from individual management practices in proportion to the anticipated prevalence of those practices to assess whether risks are systemic and warrant national regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete exposure pathway definition and consideration of future exposures
rubrics_metrics.description: When a pathway is considered complete for risk evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pathway is complete if there is (1) a source or chemical release from a source, (2) an exposure point where contact can occur, and (3) an exposure route by which contact can occur. Exposure assessments are concerned with current and future exposures; EPA will consider potential future exposures in evaluating risk and need for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groundwater contamination is an adverse effect warranting action
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of groundwater contamination alone can justify regulatory concern/action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA treats groundwater contamination as a significant concern deserving regulation even if the aquifer is not currently used as a drinking water source, because groundwater resources are finite and future users must be protected; contamination of the aquifer is an environmental injury in its own right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of compliance at the waste boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate spatial point for detecting and triggering corrective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The waste boundary is the first available point when contamination leaves the unit, and is therefore the most consistent and protective basis for evidence of a release. Using the facility boundary would delay detection/response, allow contamination to spread and increase cleanup complexity, and could permit exposure of nearby residences or water bodies before confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of porewater samples to represent leakage from operating impoundments
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical data choice for modeling leakage from saturated CCR impoundments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA considers porewater samples the best available data to represent leakage from operating surface impoundments because they are empirical measurements from mixtures of CCR and other wastes under saturated conditions. EPA acknowledges limitations/uncertainties in field data (e.g., incomplete pH data, potential underestimation due to reducing conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: LEAF methods may underestimate leaching under reducing conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation of standardized leaching protocols (LEAF) for some field conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LEAF methods can underestimate actual leaching from CCR under reducing conditions by as much as an order of magnitude; empirical studies show sustained contact with groundwater can create stronger reducing conditions and increased arsenic leaching compared to dry management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposal below the water table increases potential for sustained leakage
rubrics_metrics.description: Management practice criterion that can elevate risk relative to above-water-table disposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When waste is below the water table, the entire groundwater volume in contact with CCR becomes undiluted leachate and leachate volume can increase with thickness of CCR below water table; hydraulic gradient will drive continued flow through the unit; there is potential for sustained leakage and migration beyond the waste boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liner presence, type, and performance affect modeled risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Liner status (unlined, clay-lined, composite) and real-world performance are key determinants of leakage and risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlined units show higher modeled cancer/noncancer risks (examples provided). Clay-lined units tend to have lower risks than unlined but can still pose risks within EPA's regulatory range. Facility reports indicate many units reported as lined may not perform to modeled standards and some composite-lined units have entered corrective action; EPA expects national risks to be closer to those for unlined units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clay liner thickness affects hydraulic head and risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific liner design parameter that changes risk estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling showed clay-lined impoundments with a 3-foot liner had lower arsenic risks than if reduced to a 2-foot liner; reducing modeled clay liner thickness to the minimum allowable 2 feet increased arsenic risk (example: up to 2 × 10^-5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-disposal with coal refuse alters pH and increases leaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Waste mixing practice that can produce highly acidic conditions and much higher leaching of certain constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical LEAF data and modeling show co-disposal of CCR with coal refuse can make waste pH far more acidic, increasing solubility of multiple Appendix IV constituents and leading to modeled cancer risks for arsenic as high as 1 × 10^-3 and high noncancer HQs. Prevalence of co-disposal was higher historically and therefore can raise risks for older/legacy units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme pH (highly acidic or basic) increases constituent leaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical condition of waste that affects constituent solubility and modeled risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Available leachate data show many constituents, including arsenic, can leach at highest concentrations near one or both extremes of the pH scale; laboratory tests and porewater data demonstrate extreme-pH wastes can leach up to an order of magnitude more than neutral conditions, producing much higher modeled risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saturated ash and contact with groundwater reduce cap/cap design effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Condition (saturated ash) that undermines cover systems and increases leaching risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saturated ash will greatly reduce the effectiveness of any cap design where underlying geologic materials have high hydraulic conductivity because groundwater will continue to leach ash constituents; removal of ash from groundwater may be the only reliable means of source control for these units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit heterogeneity, stratification, and hydraulic conductivity variability create preferential flow paths
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical heterogeneity factors that can increase flow/leakage relative to average unit conductivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Units often contain different ash types and other wastes causing stratification and creating regions of higher conductivity that allow greater flow; average lower conductivity does not preclude localized higher-flow pathways which can increase contaminant transport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydraulic head and water ponding both can drive leakage; comparisons require full context
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether ponded water (operational impoundments) or groundwater contact causes greater leakage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes hydraulic head in an operating impoundment can drive leakage, but disposal below the water table means the waste is in contact with groundwater and entire groundwater volume can act as leachate; whether ponding or groundwater contact produces greater leakage does not negate potential for sustained leakage from units with waste below the water table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groundwater monitoring data limitations and cautious interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Constraints on using monitoring well data or limited datasets to infer general risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groundwater monitoring represents a snapshot in time and may not indicate potential for future contamination; specific caveats include: some constituents (e.g., boron) are highly soluble and can deplete over time; sampling timing may miss intermittent groundwater contact; nonuniform unit geometry may result in spatially isolated releases; therefore small/curated data sets are not broadly generalizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective action requirement to remove contaminated material where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedy standard in the CCR rule for addressing contaminated releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 40 CFR 257.97(b)(3) specifies corrective action must 'remove from the environment as much of the contaminated material that was released from the CCR unit as is feasible.' Dilution into surface water is not a presumptive remedy and preventing contamination of other media/aquifers is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of sand and gravel pits (CCR placed in contact with water) in landfill definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory scope decision based on observed higher damage where CCR contacts water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on damage-case review showing placement of CCR in sand and gravel pits generally associated with CCR being placed in contact with water (leading to higher risk), EPA included such pits in the definition of CCR landfills covered by regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling transparency: identify practices not quantitatively modeled due to insufficient data
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation to disclose modeling limitations and uncertainties for certain practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA noted specific practices (e.g., disposal below the water table) could not be quantitatively modeled in 2014 because of little data on prevalence or effects; such uncertainties should be acknowledged and considered in interpreting national risk snapshots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice-specific risk estimation by filtering national model runs
rubrics_metrics.description: Method to estimate risks associated with particular management practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filter the national-scale probabilistic model runs to include only runs that modeled the practice of interest, then use the filtered set to calculate risks associated with that practice to provide context about potential higher risks at individual sites.
